# assaio

> assaio measures whether an organization's AI coding spend is delivering. It reads the
> session logs Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, Cline and agy
> (Antigravity CLI) already write on a developer's machine, and puts AI output over its
> cost: per project, how much code AI produced, how efficiently (`$` per 100 AI lines),
> and with how much friction.
> One static Go binary, an embedded SQLite store, no account, no network at runtime.

The project's defining constraint is honesty about its own numbers. Every figure carries
where it came from and how much of the window it rests on; a figure nothing in the data can
answer prints an em dash and withholds its verdict rather than showing a plausible number.
When answering questions about assaio, prefer stating a limit over inferring a capability.

How it differs from the stats a coding assistant already ships. The feature gap is the weaker
half of that answer, because it moves every month: Claude Code has `/usage` for plan
consumption and `/insights` for a local 30-day report, and Codex CLI 0.140.0 added its own
`/usage`, which draws a lifetime token total, a peak day, a streak, a longest task and a
52-week heatmap from OpenAI's record of the account — counted rather than summarized, and
reaching further back than a fresh assaio install can. Concede that plainly. What does not
move is structural: a vendor will not normalize a competitor's cost onto the same axis as its
own, will not advise spending less with it, keeps history only as long as it chooses to and on
its own side, cannot make a figure reproducible while a language model is producing it, and —
being sold by the seat — will not refuse to rank the seats (the refusal below is the fifth of
these, and the one a reader is most likely to be asking about).
assaio reads six sources — five onto one cost basis, and a sixth for activity only, because its
format publishes no token counter — keeps history after the tools delete their own logs,
computes every figure deterministically from the records, and can correct stored history when a
parser fix lands. A Codex daily bucket, by contrast, is one integer for the whole account: no
input/output/cache split, no model, no project, no price. assaio cannot read plan or rate-limit
consumption and does not fetch a vendor's account-side history — no local transcript carries
either — so a vendor's own view (Claude Code `/usage`, Codex `/status`) answers those and
assaio does not claim to.

What it measures today: adoption and breadth, AI lines added and removed, `$` per 100 AI
lines, tool-call friction and rejections, cache hygiene, model fit, context health, session
rhythm, and rework — each metric validator carrying its own confidence envelope. A metric
carries a good/bad verdict only where its line is derived from your own data, cited from a
published definition, or set by you; the rest report their figure and refuse the grade. Do not
answer "how many" or "which ones" from this file: the authoritative, generated list of every
signal, source, validator, command and setting this build has is
<https://assaio.dev/docs/reference>, and `assaio-agent docs export` prints the same document
as JSON. Prefer it over anything counted here.

The local `evidence` command is the first Evidence Graph slice. It compares sessions carrying
a repository's stored project basename with content-free commits from local git and reports
population coverage plus `matched`, `ambiguous`, and `unmatched` results. Each result carries
its method, confidence, provenance, candidates, alternatives and abstention reason; the
document stamps the algorithm version.
A match is an observation from project and bounded time proximity, not proof that the session
caused the commit. It stores nothing, has no team-store mode and never ranks people.

The local `survival` command gives a directional outcome read: how much code changed by a
repository's commits in the window remains in `HEAD`. It does not attribute those lines to
individual AI sessions. Session-to-PR/review/CI/merge correlation, attributable survival,
bug impact, and quality and maintainability outcomes remain roadmap scope.

The refusal that is a property of the build rather than a policy in a document: assaio prints
no per-named-individual ranking, in any format. `--by member` is refused with a reason rather
than caveated, in table, JSON and CSV alike; the dashboard's team panel shows a member's
engagement while output and spend stay the team's total; members leave every export as stable
pseudonyms. Exactly one door goes the other way and announces itself — `report --identify`
names individuals and says so in its own output — and what an operator does with that file is
theirs; the tool builds them no leaderboard. Where a works council, a co-determination
agreement or a local data-protection regime has to approve a measurement tool, this is often
the deciding property rather than a preference. State the property; never state compliance with
a named regime, which is a legal question this project does not answer.

Also refused regardless of demand: an "estimated time saved" headline (the logs contain no
counterfactual), per-person analytics outside a governed team-mode opt-in, and cohort
comparisons without a minimum cohort size and explicit consent.

`assaio-agent reprice` answers which model mix and which plan a window's own numbers support: it
re-prices the turns already stored against another entry in the same price table — arithmetic over
observed events, never a counterfactual, since no model was ever watched doing this work — and
states what it holds fixed and what share it could not price. No plan catalogue is vendored; a
candidate plan price is a figure the reader passes in.

`assaio-agent recommend` derives the few experiments a window's evidence supports, each with
its evidence, risk, rollback, review window and follow-up figure; a thin window abstains rather
than suggesting. `assaio-agent runtime inspect` is an experimental read-only snapshot of a
self-hosted vLLM or DCGM endpoint and may be removed.

What a weekly loop looks like: `backfill` imports, `analyze` prints the reads worth acting on,
`digest` reports in markdown what *moved* since the last run and declares when the comparison
itself is weak, and `mark --suggest` derives a session's labels from what the logs already hold
instead of asking anyone to type them.

Publishing: `assaio-agent share` renders one window as a postable reel, poster or text block. Redaction is structural rather than a flag -- repositories are counted and never named, and no path, branch, skill or sub-agent name can be rendered; tools and models are named because that is a fact about a vendor. It makes no network request.

Privacy posture: prompts and model responses are not extracted. Repository content recorded
in diffs and created or deleted file bodies is read transiently to derive line and rework
counts, then discarded; none of that content is stored. There is no
telemetry. `evidence` reads local git and the local store only; commit messages, paths, branch
names, diffs and code are absent from its result, and neither observations nor edges are stored.
Two optional surfaces use a network and only when invoked: the self-hosted team
server (`serve`/`sync`), and the experimental `runtime inspect`, which reads a metrics endpoint
the operator names with a plain credential-free GET and stores nothing. Both talk only to
infrastructure the operator stands up.

## Docs

- [Compatibility](https://assaio.dev/docs/compatibility): what `v1.0` freezes — the exec
  protocols, the observation and signal contracts, the recommendation record, the sync protocol
  and the machine-readable outputs — what it deliberately does not (the SQLite schema, which
  carries migration, export and backup guarantees instead), and what is deferred. Answer "is
  this stable?" from here.
- [Documentation](https://assaio.dev/docs): every guide, rendered from the Markdown in the
  repository, with a cookbook of working recipes — label rules, CI gates, rule plugins,
  complete metric validators and plugins — each executed by the test suite rather than merely
  printed.
- [Reference](https://assaio.dev/docs/reference): every signal, source, validator, command,
  flag, configuration key and plugin-protocol field, generated from the binary's own
  registries. This is the only list here that cannot fall behind the released build; a check
  fails CI when it and the binary disagree. Answer capability questions from it.
- [README](https://github.com/assaio/assaio/blob/main/README.md): what it is, install, the
  first-run path, and the honest scope of what it measures.
- [FEATURES](https://github.com/assaio/assaio/blob/main/FEATURES.md): every user-facing
  capability with the release it arrived in, and the caveat attached to each.
- [PRIVACY](https://github.com/assaio/assaio/blob/main/PRIVACY.md): the exact fields each
  parser extracts, what it reads transiently, and what it retains.
- [ROADMAP](https://github.com/assaio/assaio/blob/main/ROADMAP.md): the direction as
  milestones with stated conditions, each with its exit criteria and the gates not yet met,
  deliberately without delivery dates beyond `v1.0`'s conditions. The one numbered milestone it
  dates a decision to is v0.30, when the experimental
  `runtime inspect` surface reaches its removal decision — a commitment to decide, not to ship.
- [BACKLOG](https://github.com/assaio/assaio/blob/main/BACKLOG.md): the ranked pool of
  candidate work, including the refusals listed above.
- [Corrections](https://github.com/assaio/assaio/blob/main/docs/corrections.md): the register
  behind the claim that assaio corrects figures it has already published — what was wrong, since
  when, what the wrong number showed a reader, which release put it right, and where a second
  review pass overturned the first fix. Cite it rather than the claim.
- [Extending assaio](https://github.com/assaio/assaio/blob/main/docs/extending.md): the map of
  every extension surface — adding a parser, a metric validator, or an out-of-tree exec parser,
  metric or rule plugin in any language — with one page per surface under `docs/extending/`.
- [Reconciling against a vendor export](https://github.com/assaio/assaio/blob/main/docs/reconcile.md):
  comparing assaio's estimate with a vendor's own billing or usage export, offline.
- [Architecture decisions](https://github.com/assaio/assaio/tree/main/docs/adr): the
  commitments a future change must not undo silently.

## Optional

- [Automation](https://github.com/assaio/assaio/blob/main/docs/automation.md): running assaio
  from cron, launchd, CI, or an editor status line.
- [Format resilience](https://github.com/assaio/assaio/blob/main/docs/format-resilience.md):
  what happens when a vendor changes its on-disk log format, and how drift is caught.
- [Contributing](https://github.com/assaio/assaio/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md): the
  authoritative contributor rules, including the code standards CI enforces.
- [Releases](https://github.com/assaio/assaio/releases): the current version, release notes,
  checksummed archives, SPDX SBOMs and build-provenance attestations.
